\chapter{Farewells}
\label{ch:farewells}
\hlchaptermodality{4}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can end a Punjabi conversation politely and choose a farewell that fits the situation.}

Complete separate oral listening and speaking checks: hear a parting and say what it promises, then part three ways yourself — the formal sat srī akāl, the everyday phir milāṁge, and the blessing rabb rākhā. Independent Gurmukhi reading and writing remain blocked until \#13068 teaches the forms.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[phir]{\pa{ਫਿਰ} (phir) — \textquotedblleft{}again,\textquotedblright{} the seed of \textquotedblleft{}see you again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PA-C04-phir}



\begin{quote}
One small word turns a goodbye from \textquotedblleft{}farewell\textquotedblright{} into \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{till next time}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਫ}} (\emph{pha}, an aspirated \emph{p}) + \textbf{\pa{ਿ}} (the \emph{sihārī}, \emph{i}-sign) + \textbf{\pa{ਰ}} (\emph{ra}) $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਫਿਰ}} (\emph{phir}).

Only \textbf{\pa{ਰ}} is yours to read so far. The other two pieces are shapes to notice, not to decode: a later session in this chapter teaches them.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਫਿਰ}} (\emph{phir}) means \textquotedblleft{}again, then, afterwards\textquotedblright{} — a native Indo-Aryan adverb (the same word as Hindi \emph{phir}) with no tidy English cognate, but a familiar \emph{job}: it turns a parting into a promise. English \textquotedblleft{}see you \textbf{again},\textquotedblright{} Punjabi \emph{phir milāṁge} (\textquotedblleft{}we'll meet \textbf{again}\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}phir\textquotedblright{} — mind the aspirated \emph{ph}
  \item what it adds to a goodbye (\textquotedblleft{}again / then\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{phir} mean, and what does it do to a farewell? (\textquotedblleft{}Again / then\textquotedblright{}; it makes the parting a promise of return.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[milāṁge]{\pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ} (milāṁge) — \textquotedblleft{}(we) will meet\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PA-C04-milaange}



\begin{quote}
A future-tense verb — the other half of \textquotedblleft{}see you again.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਮਿ}} (\emph{mi}) + \textbf{\pa{ਲਾਂ}} (\emph{lāṁ}, \emph{la} + long \emph{ā} + nasal) + \textbf{\pa{ਗੇ}} (\emph{ge}) $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ}} (\emph{milāṁge}).

You already read \textbf{\pa{ਮ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਲ}}. The rest are shapes to notice for now.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ}} (\emph{milāṁge}, \textquotedblleft{}we will meet\textquotedblright{}) is the future of \emph{milṇā} (\textquotedblleft{}to meet, to be found\textquotedblright{}), from Sanskrit \emph{mil-} (\textquotedblleft{}to join, unite\textquotedblright{}) — the root of \emph{milāp} (\textquotedblleft{}a union, meeting\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the future is an ending}]
Punjabi marks the future with an ending on the stem: \emph{mil-} (\textquotedblleft{}meet\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{-āṁge} (\textquotedblleft{}we will\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \emph{milāṁge}. No helper-word like English \textquotedblleft{}will\textquotedblright{} — the tense lives in the ending.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}milāṁge\textquotedblright{}
  \item the root and its cousin-noun (\emph{mil-} \textquotedblleft{}to join,\textquotedblright{} \emph{milāp} \textquotedblleft{}a meeting\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What verb is \emph{milāṁge} from, and how does Punjabi mark \textquotedblleft{}will\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Milṇā} \textquotedblleft{}to meet,\textquotedblright{} from Sanskrit \emph{mil-}; with the ending \emph{-āṁge}, not a separate word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[phir milāṁge]{\pa{ਫਿਰ} \pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ} (phir milāṁge) — \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PA-C04-phir-milaange}



\begin{quote}
The warm, everyday goodbye — where Chapter 1's \emph{sat srī akāl} is the formal one.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਫਿਰ} \pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ}} = \textbf{\pa{ਫਿਰ}} (\emph{phir}, \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ}} (\emph{milāṁge}, \textquotedblleft{}we will meet\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{we'll meet again}.\textquotedblright{} Chapter 1 gave you \emph{sat srī akāl}, the Sikh greeting that doubles as a formal goodbye; \emph{phir milāṁge} is the everyday, hopeful one — the same \textquotedblleft{}promise of return\textquotedblright{} the whole subcontinent prefers to a blunt farewell (Hindi \emph{phir milenge}, Bengali \emph{āshi}, Tamil \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ}). Even more casual: \emph{phir mildē hāṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}(we) meet again,\textquotedblright{} present for a near future).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the warm goodbye — \emph{phir milāṁge}
  \item the two words it's built from (\emph{phir} + \emph{milāṁge})
  \item the Hindi twin of the phrase (\emph{phir milenge})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{phir milāṁge} literally say, and when would you use it over \emph{sat srī akāl}? (\textquotedblleft{}We'll meet again\textquotedblright{}; for everyday partings, where \emph{sat srī akāl} is the formal Sikh greeting-goodbye.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{The wellbeing cycle returns at R2}

\label{lesson:PA-R04-wellbeing-r2}



\begin{quote}
Keep three oral scores: respectful question, natural reply, and courtesy close. Repair only a missed turn.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Ask:} \emph{tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?}
  \item \emph{Reply:} \emph{maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ}; then name its first-person \emph{m-} family
  \item \emph{Close:} \emph{koī gall nahīṁ}; then name the negative \emph{n-} family
\end{itemize}

\section[rabb rākhā]{\pa{ਰੱਬ} \pa{ਰਾਖਾ} (rabb rākhā) — \textquotedblleft{}God keep you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PA-C04-rab-raakha}



\begin{quote}
A tender Punjabi goodbye — one that puts you in God's care.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਰੱਬ}} (\emph{rabb}, \textquotedblleft{}God\textquotedblright{} — note the \emph{addak} doubling on \textbf{\pa{ੱਬ}}) + \textbf{\pa{ਰਾਖਾ}} (\emph{rākhā}, \textquotedblleft{}keeper, protector\textquotedblright{}). Both words open with the \textbf{\pa{ਰ}} you already read.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਰੱਬ} \pa{ਰਾਖਾ}} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{{[}may{]} God {[}be your{]} keeper}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{rabb} (\textquotedblleft{}God\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{rākhā} (\textquotedblleft{}protector,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{rakhṇā}, \textquotedblleft{}to keep, protect,\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{rakṣ-}, \textquotedblleft{}to guard,\textquotedblright{} the root of \emph{rākṣas} and of English-borrowed \emph{rakhi}). The word for God, \textbf{\pa{ਰੱਬ}} (\emph{rabb}), is itself telling: it is \textbf{Arabic} \emph{rabb} (\textquotedblleft{}lord, master\textquotedblright{}) — the same \emph{rabb} of Arabic \emph{rabb al-ʿālamīn} (\textquotedblleft{}Lord of the worlds\textquotedblright{}). So this most Punjabi of farewells fuses an \textbf{Arabic} name for God with a \textbf{Sanskrit} verb of keeping — Punjabi's two vocabularies in one blessing. Warmer still: \emph{rabb rākhā, phir milāṁge} (\textquotedblleft{}God keep you, we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rabb rākhā\textquotedblright{}
  \item its two heritages (Arabic \emph{rabb} \textquotedblleft{}God\textquotedblright{} + Sanskrit \emph{rakṣ-} \textquotedblleft{}to keep\textquotedblright{})
  \item pair it with the other goodbye — \emph{rabb rākhā, phir milāṁge}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{rabb rākhā} mean, and what two vocabularies meet in it? (\textquotedblleft{}God {[}be your{]} keeper\textquotedblright{}; Arabic \emph{rabb} \textquotedblleft{}God\textquotedblright{} + Sanskrit \emph{rakṣ-} \textquotedblleft{}to protect.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pha · ga · -i]{\pa{ਫ} · \pa{ਗ} · \pa{ਿ} — three pieces met inside a word you already say}

\label{lesson:PA-S04-phappha-gagga}



\begin{quote}
The first word of this chapter is three pieces long, and the last one arrives today.

First, say the last things you learned once more, out loud and from memory:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ṭhīk} · \emph{koī gall nahīṁ}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \pa{ਫ} · \pa{ਗ} · \pa{ਿ}}
\begin{quote}
\pa{ਫ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{phapphā} — \emph{pha}. A consonant with a puff of breath after it — \emph{p} plus an audible \emph{h}, not the \emph{f} of English \emph{phone}.

\begin{quote}
\pa{ਗ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{gaggā} — \emph{ga}. A consonant, the voiced \emph{g} of \emph{go}, with no breath after it.

\begin{quote}
\pa{ਿ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{sihārī} — \emph{-i}. A mātrā for short \emph{i}, and the one that surprises everybody: it is \textbf{written before} the consonant it is \textbf{spoken after}.

Now put them where you have already heard them:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਫ}} + \textbf{\pa{ਿ}} + \textbf{\pa{ਰ}} $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਫਿਰ}} (\emph{phir})
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਫਿਰ}} — \emph{phir} — \textbf{again, then}
\end{quote}

You are not being asked to write any of this. You are being asked to \textbf{recognise} it the next time it goes past.

\subsection*{Writing: copy what you can see}
Keep \pa{ਫ} · \pa{ਗ} · \pa{ਿ} in front of you and do not cover any of them. Follow each shape once with a finger, then copy it once with a pencil, larger than it is printed. Say its sound as your hand stops.

\begin{quote}
This is \textbf{observe-and-trace with the model visible}. Nothing in these chapters asks you to write a Punjabi word from memory; that ladder starts later, and it starts from these same shapes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\pa{ਫਿਰ}} and point to each of today's pieces in turn
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pha}, \emph{ga}, \emph{-i}, then the whole word — \emph{phir}
  \item \emph{Look:} back at the headword at the top of any earlier lesson in this chapter and find one shape you now know
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name today's pieces: \emph{phapphā}, \emph{gaggā}, \emph{sihārī}. Which of them is a \textbf{mātrā} or a mark rather than a letter, and what does \textbf{\pa{ਫਿਰ}} say? (\emph{phir}, “again, then”.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A00.pdf}{Unicode Gurmukhi chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 4 — The farewells}

\label{lesson:PA-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three ways to part, from the formal to the tender.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — three ways to part}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the formal Sikh greeting-goodbye (Chapter 1) — \emph{sat srī akāl}
  \item the everyday \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{} — \emph{phir milāṁge}
  \item the blessing \textquotedblleft{}God keep you\textquotedblright{} — \emph{rabb rākhā}
  \item the two together — \emph{rabb rākhā, phir milāṁge}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn — the atoms}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}(we) will meet\textquotedblright{} (\emph{phir}, \emph{milāṁge})
  \item \emph{Say it:} the ending that carries \textquotedblleft{}we will\textquotedblright{} (\emph{-āṁge})
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\pa{ਫਿਰ}} and name the three pieces this chapter taught you — \emph{phapphā}, \emph{gaggā}, \emph{sihārī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{milāṁge} $\leftarrow$ \emph{mil-} \textquotedblleft{}to join\textquotedblright{} (\emph{milāp}, \textquotedblleft{}a meeting\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{rabb} $\leftarrow$ Arabic \textquotedblleft{}Lord/God\textquotedblright{}; \emph{rākhā} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{rakṣ-} \textquotedblleft{}to protect\textquotedblright{}
  \item the future \emph{-āṁge} ending — \textquotedblleft{}we will,\textquotedblright{} carried in the verb
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You're leaving a friend and expect to see them soon. Give the warm goodbye, then bless them on the way. (\emph{Phir milāṁge} — and \emph{rabb rākhā}.)

Independent Gurmukhi reading and writing are \textbf{not scored here}. Romanization is evidence for spoken recall only; a typed romanization never counts as Gurmukhi writing.
\end{tcolorbox}
